Learning Objectives
Discuss the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for nursemaids elbow injuries.
Perform an appropriate workup for pediatric patients in whom a fracture about the elbow is
suspected.
Review the management of nursemaids elbow.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Commonly observed in children aged 2 to 3 years
Longitudinal traction on the elbow causes radial head subluxation.
Most can be managed via closed reduction without immobilization.


Overview
Radial head subluxation (nursemaids elbow) is a common injury typically observed in
children aged 2 to 3 years because of longitudinal traction on the forearm. It generally is
managed via gentle closed reduction and does not typically require immobilization or
additional management. Some children sustain repeated subluxation events of the
radial head; in these children, a brief period of immobilization in a long arm cast may be
warranted to prevent recurrence.1
Epidemiology
Approximately 60% to 65% of cases occur in females.
Most commonly occurs in children aged 2 to 3 years.
Rare in children older than 7 years

Epidemiology
Radial head subluxation occurs with longitudinal traction on the outstretched arm of a
child younger than 5 years. The annular, or orbicular, ligament slides over the radial
head, causing subluxation of the radiocapitellar joint. Although this is a very common
injury, the true incidence is difficult to determine because many of these injuries are
managed in pediatric clinics, urgent care clinics, or emergency departments by non-
orthopaedic providers. It occurs more commonly in females.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The elbow follows a sequential pattern of ossification and fusion (Figure 1; Table 1).

On AP radiographs, slight lateral angulation of the proximal radial metaphysis is observed
(mean of 12.5°). This angulation is normal and should not be mistaken for a fracture.2
The ossific nucleus of the radius also can be bipartite, which is a normal anatomic variation
and also should not be mistaken for a fracture.1,3
Joints and Ligaments
No direct soft-tissue attachments to the radial head or neck exist.

Joints and Ligaments
The annular ligament wraps circumferentially around the radial neck but arises from the
radial side of the ulna. This ligament also is the attachment site for the radial (lateral)
collateral ligaments. The annular ligament and the lateral collateral ligaments stabilize
the radiocapitellar joints and protect against varus stress1 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Illustrations of an elbow show the structure of the medial collateral ligament
complex (A) and the lateral collateral ligament complex (B). (Reproduced from Tashjian
RZ, Katarincic JA: Complex elbow instability. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14[5]:278-86.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Nursemaids Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004068
4/10


Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Longitudinal traction on the pediatric forearm allows the annular ligament to slide over
the radial head and into the radiocapitellar joint. If the forearm is in pronation, the radial
head is narrow and has a rounded margin, which predisposes the ligament to instability
if longitudinal traction is applied with the forearm in the position. If the forearm is in
supination, the radial head is wider and the joint is more stable, decreasing the risk of
annular ligament translocation in this position.1
Risk Factors

Risk Factors
Studies have shown that children with hypermobility are predisposed to radial head
subluxation during childhood, and an increased likelihood exists that one or both
parents also have hypermobility.4
Associated Injuries
No associated injuries in most patients with radial head subluxation/nursemaids elbow.
Injury Classification
No classification scheme exists for this injury.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
The Patient history and physical examination are classic, with the child holding the elbow
extended and the forearm pronated.
Patient History
SEND FEEDBACK


Patient History
These injuries tend to occur in otherwise healthy children who have sustained a
longitudinal traction force on the forearm with the elbow in an extended position.
Common mechanisms of injury include a parent or guardian pulling up a child by the
forearms/wrists or pulling a child across a street. Very young children may only briefly
complain of pain before attempting to return to regular activities; however, the
parent/guardian notices that the child persistently ignores the affected arm, holding the
extremity in adduction with the elbow slightly flexed and the forearm pronated. The
parent/guardian will notice that the child refuses to use the affected extremity,
preferring to use the unaffected extremity and resisting attempts at elbow range of
motion.
Physical Examination

Physical Examination
The child typically presents with the affected elbow slightly flexed and the forearm
slightly pronated. The radiocapitellar joint may be mildly tender to palpation. In patients
with an isolated injury, swelling, ecchymosis, and other soft-tissue changes are
uncommon. Neurologic and vascular injuries have not been reported with an isolated
radial head subluxation, and the extremity should be neurovascularly intact on
examination.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs are not necessary unless the classic patient history and arm positioning are
absent. If radiographs are obtained, they appear normal. CT and MRI typically are not
necessary for either diagnosis or management of these injuries.

Ultrasonography
May demonstrate increased distance between the radial head and the capitellum

Imaging Studies
Gentle closed reduction usually is successful, and imaging studies typically are not
warranted for diagnosis. However, ultrasonography can be performed to evaluate the
radiocapitellar joint, and the normal radiocapitellar joint distance is 3.8 mm.5 An
increased radiocapitellar joint distance may be diagnostic of interposition of the annular
ligament; however, such imaging typically is not warranted.1
Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
Differential diagnoses include a nondisplaced fracture of the proximal radius, a
Monteggia fracture with plastic deformation of the ulna, and an annular ligament tear.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
This is the preferred treatment approach for all nursemaids elbows and generally is successful.
Techniques/Procedures
Gentle longitudinal traction, while taking the forearm through supination and pronation, and
elbow flexion and extension should reduce all acute nursemaids elbows.
Nonsurgical Fracture Fixation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Nursemaids Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004068
7/10

No fixation is required; however, in children with recurrent subluxation events, a brief period
of immobilization (approximately 2 to 3 weeks) in a splint or cast may help prevent
recurrence.1
Outcomes
Outcomes are believed to be good; however, no long-term follow-up studies have been
performed in children with a history of nursemaids elbow.
After successful closed reduction, the child typically will attempt to resume normal elbow and
forearm range of motion without restriction; however, if the nursemaids elbow remains
unreduced, the child may have some continued pain and hesitancy with elbow range of
motion after reduction. In this circumstance, the provider should obtain radiographs to rule
out an occult fracture; if these radiographs appear normal, the child should be briefly
immobilized and then reexamined. Often, after a brief period of immobilization, the pain will
have completely resolved and the child will be able to resume full range of motion of the
forearm and elbow without pain.
Surgical Management
Indications
Surgical management is not warranted. In the rare circumstance of a radial head subluxation
in which closed reduction fails in a patient with a diagnosis of nursemaids elbow, the surgeon
must consider alternate diagnoses, such as a missed Monteggia fracture or an annular
ligament tear or interposition.
Surgical technique is based on the underlying pathology preventing reduction of the radial
head.
Contraindications
Surgical management should not be attempted without a trial of closed reduction. Because
closed reduction is almost always successful, imaging studies, including radiographs and MRIs,
ultrasonographic images, or other imaging studies to evaluate the elbow joint, are warranted
to confirm the diagnosis and treatment plan before proceeding with surgical management.
Complications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Nursemaids Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004068
8/10

Recurrent nursemaids elbow is relatively common in children younger than 5 years. Patients
with recurrent nursemaids elbow often have signs of generalized ligamentous laxity (elbow
hyperextension, positive thumb to forearm sign, metacarpophalangeal hyperextension to 90°).
Families should be counseled on avoiding any longitudinal traction on the arm. Fortunately,
most recurrent nursemaids elbows stabilize during grade school.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Providers should never assume that a child with elbow pain who sustained an unwitnessed fall
has nuresmaids elbow. In the absence of the typical patient history of longitudinal traction on
an extended forearm/elbow, the provider must critically evaluate the patient for an occult
fracture via a thorough physical examination and pertinent radiographs.
